title: Building America’s new power grid | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Episode summary of an ACORE-sponsored Energy Gang podcast recorded at the ACORE Grid Forum: guests from Grid United, the Regulatory Assistance Project, Clearway Energy and ACORE argue that US transmission build-out is held back by permitting, cost-allocation disputes and interconnection queues, pointing to inter-regional transmission, Great Britain's cap-and-floor model and Southwest Power Pool's interconnection reforms as fixes. The page is a short episode description, not a transcript.

insights.claim: Data centres for AI and new chip and battery factories are driving up US electricity demand on an already-struggling grid, and there is broad cross-sector, cross-partisan agreement that new transmission is urgently needed but power lines remain hard to build.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Consensus need plus execution friction means transmission is a constrained, high-value asset class for those who can get projects permitted.
insights.quote: getting new power lines built remains a major challenge
insights.locator: Americas needs more electricity, and fast.

insights.claim: Key barriers discussed at the ACORE Grid Forum were lengthy permitting, uncertain project costs and market rules no longer fit for purpose when new generation must connect quickly.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Regulatory reform, not capital availability, is the gating variable for grid capex.
insights.quote: market rules that are no longer fit for purpose

insights.claim: Madeline Gould Laughlin of Grid United argues grid operators undervalue the reliability benefits of inter-regional transmission and should recognize them to give utilities stronger incentives to build connections.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Rule changes valuing inter-regional reliability would unlock merchant long-distance lines like Grid United's.
insights.locator: Ed is joined first by Madeline

insights.claim: Jenny Chen of the Regulatory Assistance Project highlights Great Britain's cap-and-floor transmission funding model, combining developer revenue certainty with incentives for commercial success, as a possible template for the US, where states and grid operators struggle to agree who pays.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A cap-and-floor regime would de-risk transmission returns and attract infrastructure capital.

insights.claim: Adam Stern of Clearway Energy says uncertain connection costs and long interconnection queues are keeping new supply offline, and points to Southwest Power Pool reforms giving developers more cost certainty as a model for other grid operators.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: SPP could become a favored region for new generation development if its interconnection reforms work.

insights.claim: Colin Meehan of ACORE argues stronger inter-regional connections would improve reliability, unlock lower-cost power and help keep consumer bills down, and that state and regional work remains essential regardless of federal bipartisan permitting reform.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Investors should not bank solely on federal permitting reform; state-level progress drives actual project timelines.
insights.locator: Finally, Ed speaks to Colin Meehan

insights.claim: The common conclusion is that grid expansion investment opportunities are real but regulatory barriers, financing challenges and slow development continue to hold projects back.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Grid investment upside is gated on converting political consensus into regulatory action.
insights.quote: the investment opportunities to expand grid capacity are real, but regulatory barriers, financing challenges and slow development processes continue to hold projects back
insights.locator: Across the conversations, a common challenge
